speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ABOLITION OF RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTS OF INDUSTRIAL CHEMICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to advise the house that the United Kingdom government has announced today its decision to abolish restrictions on imports of industrial chemicals from Canada and other dollar countries. This major new measure of relaxation is to take effect on August 18. These discriminatory restrictions have been an impediment to the development of our trade in this field for many years.
With only a few exceptions, all Canadian chemicals and allied products of a kind used industrially will now be completely free of import controls in the United Kingdom. They include a number of important chemical products with respect to which we have been seeking improved access to the United Kingdom market.
Total Canadian exports of industrial chemicals in this field amounted in 1957 to some $130 million, of which about 10 per cent went to the United Kingdom. With the removal of restrictions our producers and exporters will be in a position to compete freely in the United Kingdom without quantitative limitation, and we are hopeful that this may lead to a substantial increase in our chemical exports to Britain.

I am sure we all welcome this response by the United Kingdom government to the representations we have been making to them. These new measures are a major contribution by the United Kingdom toward providing new opportunities for expanding trade between our two countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: SALTED COD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past several weeks a number of questions have been raised in this house concerning the 1958 production and marketing of salted cod. This product is of major significance to the economy and the fishermen of Newfoundland, Quebec and the maritime provinces.
Much of the concern expressed by members of this house and by all branches of the industry arose from reports that from 1,500 to 2,000 additional fishermen would be operating in Newfoundland this year. There was also fear that above average stocks of 1957 fish would be carried over into the new marketing year.
The whole question was reviewed by the fisheries prices support board here in Ottawa

on July 22 and July 23. The board found that considerable improvement had occurred in the statistical position from a marketing point of view. It is now estimated that the 1958 production, even under most favourable conditions for the balance of the fishing season, will not exceed that of 1957. Furthermore, stocks have been reduced to normal levels for this time of year.
In view of these developments and bearing in mind that production in most competing countries is not yet known, the board decided to adjourn its meeting and will meet again early in September in Halifax and St. John's. At that time the board should be in a position to make a recommendation to the government based on more complete facts.
While prices to fishermen have not yet been set for the 1958 production, the board feels that in view of the reduced supply position commercial market prices will be established at much better levels than were previously anticipated. I have asked the board to watch the situation very carefully, and I can assure the fishermen that their interests will be constantly borne in mind.
In so far as the marketing aspect of the problem is concerned, the position is much improved over what it was a few weeks ago.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to amplify an answer I gave to a question addressed to me by the Leader of the Opposition on Saturday last. The question asked was as follows:
In view of the Prime Minister's statement last night calling for an increase of $3 billion in the resources of the international monetary fund and a very large increase in the lending capacity of the international bank, can the minister tell us whether the Canadian delegation to the economic and social council of the United Nations, which is currently meeting at Geneva, has been instructed to pursue these important objectives and, if so, with what result?
The interim answer which I gave on Saturday last was in part as follows:
I am not clear that this is a matter for representation to the economic and social council. We are represented on the boards of the international bank and the monetary fund.
To this answer I would like to add the following statement. The annual reports of the monetary fund and of the world bank are considered by the economic and social council, as the hon. member knows. However, this item was on the agenda of the council at its 25th session in New York last spring, not at the current session. Normally, the affairs of these two bodies are not studied at the summer session, the meeting now under way in Geneva. In any event the membership of the economic and social council is such that no very useful purpose would be served by seeking to have these matters discussed in that forum.
It will, I think, be readily appreciated that the ideas put forward by the Prime Minister could more appropriately be explored in the first instance within the organizations involved, that is to say the international monetary fund and the international bank.
Canada is represented on the boards of those two organizations. Those meetings will be held in New Delhi beginning October 6.

Maybe a little bit of politics enters into the matter, but not enough to do any harm.
What we need in this country is a provision for farm loans up to at least 90 per cent of the appraised value. As the situation is at present in Ontario and part of Quebec -and I think the same is true to some extent in all parts of Canada-the appraiser appraises the buildings at nothing. He fixes the value at $8,000, and that is only on the house. If it were in a small village like my own or in a place like Eastview near Ottawa, that building would be worth $10,000, but it is on a farm and so the valuation is less. As for the big barn and the other buildings, they do not allow much; they just put on a small valuation.

Most of the appraisals are made by good, sound appraisers. But when the appraised value is only $8,000, and loans will be made up to only 60 per cent of the appraised value, therefore you could get a loan on 100 acres of $5,000 to $6,000. They cannot do anything with that when consideration is given to the cost of farm machinery and equipment, which is high. A good Liberal government introduced legislation providing loans for the purchase of machines and the repairs of buildings, but the Conservative government has done nothing up to now. The situation is worse now than it was before.
I shall be happy to see this bill passed as quickly as possible. I hope that my good friend the Minister of Agriculture will have a free hand to lend money through the Minister of Finance and through the cabinet, because right now the people need more credit than they ever needed it before. Machinery and things of that sort are very expensive.
As to the rate of interest it should not be a cent more than 4 per cent. If you want to help the farmer that is the only way to do it. Provision should also be made for loans up to at least 90 per cent of the first $10,000 of valuation. The rate of interest should be 4 per cent and repayment should be spread over 30 years, with the possibility of repaying at any time without notice. I will give full credit to the experts of the government, because we have good men in the federal Department of Agriculture, first class men, and we also have good men in the department of agriculture of Ontario. I am speaking for Ontario right now. We have good and clever people who carry on to the best of their ability.
What we need is the same thing we have for our veterans under the Veterans' Land Act. We need experts to go out to these farmers and tell them gently and quietly how best to carry on. Give a chance to these farmers to produce more. No doubt they will not say that because some are afraid of the vote, but for 50 per cent of the farmers I know, if they had these experts from the federal government and the provincial government they could be educated, if I may use that word. In French I will use another... (Translation):
-helping those people to improve their farming methods, to take better care of their livestock, they would, I believe, increase their income by 50 to 100 per cent.

I will not delay the bill. I should be more pleased if it provided for more, because after all we lend money to everybody. If there is a good place to lend money it is to those on the farm. If we do not keep our farmers prosperous the country will not be prosperous, and the government will go more deeply into debt. I
should like to draw the attention of the minister to a weakness that appears to exist, not so much in the Canadian Farm Loan Act itself as in the interpretation or administration of the act in the field at the level where an applicant first makes his application for a loan.
On the basis of complaints that have arisen among the farm organizations in my riding it would appear that those who first receive these applications in the department tend to find existing debt a deterrent to a loan, without sufficiently taking into account the ability of the farmer applicant to repay principal and interest. It would appear that the first consideration in dealing with an application would be ability to repay, yet on the basis of the experience of people at least in my own riding there is a hesitation to consider an application where debt exists and a tendency not to give sufficient consideration to ability to repay.
In many cases a farmer seeks a loan for the purpose of consolidating debts, to transfer or exchange short-term debt for long-term debt at a rate of interest and over a period of time more within his capability of paying. But so long as that debt exists apparently there is a hesitation on the part of the officials in the field to consider a loan. I know of cases where farmers have been told that when they have cleaned up existing debt the farm loan board will consider their application; yet if they were in a position to clean up existing debt there would be no necessity for an application in the first place.
Consequently I feel that possibly the intention of the act is not being fulfilled if officials do not give first consideration to ability to repay and only in that regard consider an application, and not permit themselves to be put off consideration by the fact that debt exists. Many farmers over a period of time,

particularly in recent years, have resorted to short-term borrowing at fairly high interest rates. The act provides them with the means of changing, but many of those who have sought to make the change have found that simply because of interpretation they have been unable to do so.
If that aspect of the administration of this act were given consideration, to see whether there is justification for perhaps a direction to officials to consider the aspect of repayment rather than the aspect of debt, a very great service may be done to many farmers without any change whatever in existing legislation.

I realize, however, that members were given some assurance that the general subject of agricultural credit is being carefully reviewed by the government.
I would like to point out, however, in view of the fact that such statements were made as long as a year ago, that this is an urgent problem and one which should be dealt with. I rather thought there would be more in the bill than simply a change of capitalization for the purpose of increasing the possible amount of borrowing from the government. I share the views of those who have spoken in that it is a fine thing to see additional credit facilities being developed, but I am sure the Minister of Finance himself would be the first to say that the actual extent of the rate of increase, either in the amount of new lending or the amount of the average loan, has been about the same between 1956

The act says that the interest rate is not fixed under the act itself but is an interest rate which in the opinion of the board is sufficient to provide for the interest payable by the board to the minister's department plus the expenses of the board.
I noted that while one or two members of the committee advocated, as was also done in 1956, that this form of lending should be conducted at an interest rate which would involve a substantial subsidy from the taxpayers of the country, the Minister of Finance pointed out, as did the chairman of the board, that a very slight reduction in the present interest rate of 5 per cent would completely wipe out the surplus on the operations of the board. I believe the chairman of the board said that one-tenth of one per cent would be about the equivalent of the surplus for last year on the board's operations.
I am not going to criticize unduly the minister or anyone else but, while I was not a member of the committee, it did seem to me as I was reading the material we all receive that it was rather unfortunate that the actual printed report of the board was available or tabled in the house only a day or two after the committee on agriculture and colonization had concluded its sittings. I am not for one moment suggesting that the committee was denied any information, but I do suggest to the minister something to which I am sure he will give careful study, and that is that if the actual report is just about ready it would be so much more helpful if it could be made available to the house when legislation is in the resolution stage or on second reading, because of course there are a great number of members of the house who are not members of the committee which is going into the details of such matters, and I am sure that at this stage of the session it is the desire of all of us not to be unduly repetitious.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak on this amendment to the farm loan act, and it is not my intention to cover what was said by the Minister of Finance when he introduced the amendment. I would, however, like to express my satisfaction and that of the people I have the honour to represent with respect to this amendment to the act and what it means to us. The change is long overdue, because since the bill was introduced some years ago conditions in our farm industry have considerably changed; methods of farming, the value of our farm lands, the price of our farm equipment and so on have all undergone changes.
By making it possible for the farm loan board to borrow another $40 million from the federal government it will mean that many more applicants will receive loans and, according to the chairman of the farm loan board, a greater demand for these loans in coming years is foreseen. At the present time there is a $15,000 limit upon the amount which a farmer can borrow from the board. Some are of the opinion that this amount is not large enough, and that it should be raised to $20,000. Others are of the opinion that it should be left at $15,000 because no farmer can borrow his way into prosperity, and because credit is not the cure for all our troubles.
However, I am confident that in due time this matter also will receive consideration by the government. I base this belief on what has happened here in the last few days. It is very significant that so many amendments have been introduced in the last few days to measures pertaining to agriculture. For instance, the Prairie Farm Assistance

Canadian Farm Loan Act Act was amended, with the result that many complaints will toe removed; the Animal Contagious Diseases Act was amended also, and only recently the act making possible cash advances to farmers was amended to give a better service to our Canadian farmers.

We will, I am sure, be very interested in the working of this act when it has been passed into law. I am in favour of the amendment, and will give it my support.

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution: That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Financial Administration Act to authorize the deletion from the accounts of obligations or debts due to Her Majesty or claims by Her Majesty that do not exceed twenty-five dollars; to clarify the circumstances in which special warrants signed by the governor general may be issued; to permit a crown corporation to establish a receiver general account with ministerial approval and to authorize the payment of interest on money placed to the credit of such an account; and to provide for certain consequential changes in connection with the administration of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE DELETION OF CERTAIN ACCOUNTS, CLARIFY ISSUE OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S WARRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
the purpose of the bill to be founded upon the present resolution is to amend the provisions of the Financial Administration Act. The bill will be a quite short one and will have as its objects, first, to authorize the treasury board to make regulations for the deletion from the government's books of small debts of $25 or less; second, to clarify the circumstances under which special governor general's warrants may be used and to provide an opportunity for prompt parliamentary consideration of those warrants when they are used; third, to permit a crown corporation, with ministerial approval, to pay all or part of its money into the consolidated revenue fund to be held for it by the receiver general and to provide for the payment of interest on moneys so held, and, fourthly, to make certain other technical and consequential changes.
The operative provisions of section 28 of the act relating to the circumstances and conditions governing the use of special warrants restrict their use to cases;
(a)	where an accident happens to a public work or building for which an expenditure for the repair or renewal thereof is urgently required, and
(b)	where any other matter arises for which an expenditure not foreseen or provided for by parliament is urgently required for the public good.
Moreover, warrants may be used only in periods when parliament is not in session or when it is under adjournment sine die or to a day more than two weeks after the day the accident happens or the matter arises.
The wording of the act, which has remained virtually unchanged since provision for the use of special warrants was made shortly after confederation, has been found in some respects to be lacking in
Financial Administration Act clarity. Accordingly, these provisions have been rewritten in the bill to simplify the language and to clarify the circumstances in which warrants may be issued. I should like to stress that no change in substance has been made. As under the present act, warrants can be used only when parliament is not in session or is under adjournment, when there is no other appropriation for the service, and when expenditures are urgently required for the public good.
As I have indicated, it is also proposed to make provision to give hon. members an early opportunity for the consideration of special warrants when they are issued. There are now two requirements enacted by parliament to ensure that the existence of governor general's warrants may be made known soon after they are issued. These are to be found in sub-section (3) of section 28:
Every warrant issued under this section shall be published in the Canada Gazette within thirty days after it is issued, and a statement showing all warrants issued under this section and the amounts thereof shall be laid by the minister before the House of Commons within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session of parliament.
We are proposing no change in these requirements. However, we do propose to add a new provision whereby the amounts appropriated by a special warrant shall be deemed to be included in, and not to be in addition to, the amounts provided by the next appropriation act enacted by parliament. The effect will be that provision to cover all such warrants will be included in the first appropriation act submitted to parliament in the session following the period in which the warrants are issued, and the house will thereby be given a full and early opportunity to consider such warrants.
In addition to these amendments relating to the use of special governor general's warrants, there are three other amendments to the act, mostly of a technical nature, which I should like to mention.
The first relates to the deletion of certain small debts due to, or claims by, Her Majesty. Section 23 of the act now provides that the governor in council on the recommendation of the treasury board may delete from the accounts certain obligations or debts due to, or claims by, Her Majesty that do not exceed $500 and which have been outstanding for five years or more, or that do not exceed $1,000 and have been outstanding for ten years or more.
It is costly and uneconomical to continue to maintain records and to seek actively to collect very small debts for the period of five years now required by the act. Indeed in

Financial Administration Act many cases the cost of administration and collection exceeds the amount of the debt, and it has become evident that there should be some procedure under appropriate circumstances for dealing more expeditiously with these small uncollectable debts. Accordingly, vote 689 was included in the further supplementary estimates (2), 1957-1958 to provide authority for the treasury board to make regulations for the deletion from the accounts of small debts that did not exceed $5. We do not propose to include this item in the final appropriation act for 1957-58. Instead, it is proposed that it be placed on a statutory basis by making suitable provision in the Financial Administration Act. At the same time it is proposed that the maximum amount that may be deleted under this authority will be $25. A report of all amounts deleted under this provision will be published each year in the public accounts.
The second amendment which I should like to mention refers to the making of regulations for the destruction of paid government cheques. Section 34(2) of the act now provides that the treasury board on the recommendation of the auditor general may make regulations governing the destruction of paid and cancelled cheques or similar instruments issued by the comptroller of the treasury for payments out of the consolidated revenue fund. I do not believe that the auditor general should be responsible for proposing regulations governing administrative action. On the other hand it is most desirable to ensure that cheques are not destroyed until they are no longer required by him for the purposes of his examination and audit of the public accounts. Accordingly I am proposing that the present section be amended to provide that in future regulations governing the destruction of paid cheques be made by the treasury board on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance with the approval of the auditor general.
There is one other amendment to the act which will permit a crown corporation, with ministerial approval, to establish a receiver general account. Section 81(2) now provides that a crown corporation, when directed by the Minister of Finance with the concurrence of the appropriate minister, shall pay all or any part of its money to the receiver general to be held for it in a special account in the consolidated revenue fund and such money may be paid out for the purposes of the corporation or repaid to it. It is proposed that this section be amended so that a crown corporation may on its own initiative but with the approval of the two ministers pay surplus money to the receiver general to be held for it in the special account. Specific 

provision is also being made in this section to make it clear that interest may be allowed and paid on such money.
These are the amendments which I am proposing. I believe that they will clarify and improve the provisions of the present legislation.

the second reading of Bill No. S-12, respecting Ogdensburg Bridge Authority.
He said: This bill is similar to the bill passed in 1956. The Ogdensburg bridge authority was incorporated by private act of the parliament of Canada, being chapter 57 of the statutes of 1952. The purpose of the authority is to co-operate with a similar authority incorporated by the legislature of the state of New York in the building of a high-level vehicular bridge from the vicinity of Johnstown, Ontario, that is about two miles east of Prescott, to Ogdensburg, New York.
When the company was incorporated in 1952 it was estimated that the bridge would cost approximately $10 million to $12 million and accordingly the right of the company to borrow and to issue bonds, debentures or other securities was limited by sections 12, 16 and 17 of the act of incorporation. By the year 1955 it became apparent that the original estimates of the cost of the bridge

were low and accordingly at the 1956 session an amending act was passed, being chapter 65 of the statutes of 1956, increasing the amount of debentures or other securities which could be issued and the amount which could be borrowed to $20 million. It now appears that the bridge will in fact cost more than $20 million but less than $25 million, and accordingly the present application is to obtain authority to borrow or issue debentures or securities to an amount not exceeding $25 million. This is the sole and only purpose of the bill which follows the exact terms of the 1956 bill.
I should like to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that the act of incorporation provides that when the cost of building the bridge has been retired, that portion of it over Canadian soil will revert to public authorities in Canada and that part of the bridge in the United States of America will revert to public authorities in the United States. In other words, this is not an undertaking for the financial gain of any private individual.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that the tenders are practically all let for this bridge at the present time and the authority finds that the increase in the cost of labour from 1952 to the present time and the increase in the cost of materials used will mean that the bridge will cost in the neighbourhood of $22 million. It is for this reason the bill is being brought before the house and Senate at the present time, seeking authority to borrow or issue debentures or securities to an amount not exceeding $25 million. This is a very short bill. It has already passed the Senate. The construction work is proceeding rapidly, so it is the desire of those concerned that this bill be passed at the earliest possible opportunity.

the second reading of Bill No. S-13, respecting The Algoma Central and Hudson Bay Railway Company.
He said: If I may give to the house a brief outline of the purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, I would say that there is a rather lengthy explanation note contained in the bill. Primarily, this concerns a refinancing scheme of this company. The Algoma Central and Hudson Bay Railway Company was incorporated by chapter 50 of the statues of Canada in 1899. The company has constructed and operates a line of railway from
Private Bills
the city of Sault Ste. Marie to Hearst in the province of Ontario, and a branch line thereof running in a southwesterly direction to Michipicoten Harbour in the province of Ontario.
As I said, the purpose of this bill is to reorganize the capital structure of the company which has had a long and somewhat complicated history. In 1916 a compromise financial arrangement was made by the company, other companies and the bondholders, but the obligations of this scheme were not met in 1931, at which time a new scheme was arranged. At that time the scheme was confirmed by chapter 62 of the statutes of Canada. Under that scheme the bonded indebtedness of the company was to consist of $10,308,500, bearing interest at the rate of five per cent and being secured by first mortgage debentures on the stocks and bonds.
I might say a trust deed, and the usual type documents were made at that time to secure the interest of the bondholders. Also a second mortgage of $318,800, bearing interest at six per cent, was authorized, but this was paid off in 1937.
The company was further authorized to issue preference shares to the amount of $500,000 which provided 125,000 shares at $4 each. Under the present arrangement the proposal is to pay off the indebtedness which becomes due on December 31, 1959; to pay off the present preferred shares and to pay off the accumulated interest which, as at June 2, 1958, amounted to $5,729,808. Under a further scheme which was authorized in 1941 the company was authorized to allow the interest to accumulate provided that interest was paid when the bonds came due.
As a result of the scheme, when it is passed by the house, it will also permit the addition of further common shares. There will be a total capital authorized as follows: common shares to the value of $10 million, being 1 million shares having a par value of $10 each; preferred shares to the amount of $12,500,000, being 250,000 shares having a par value of $50; and the raising of $11 million by bonds and debentures. This procedure will completely reorganize the capital structure of the company. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-19, to amend the Canada Elections Act (publication of straw poll results).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this amendment is to prohibit and make punishable as an illegal practice the publication in any manner before election day the result of straw polls or polls on the political opinions of the electors. The proposed amendment does not prohibit the taking of such polls for private purposes and it should be pointed out that we in this group have no objection to the taking of polls of political opinions of the public. We have no objection to the taking of such polls in high schools or public schools or in any other places but what we do object to is the publication of the results of those polls to be used for purposes other than that for which they were intended when the poll was originally taken. Some consideration has been given to this matter by other countries and by certain provinces in Canada, which have passed legislation prohibiting such use of polls.
Something should, I think, be said with regard to what may be accomplished by the taking of polls and the results which sometimes may be found from the conducting of them. We all know of cases where questions are asked of the general public which are very innocent in nature but by the time the results of such polls are used by certain advertising agencies and implications are drawn from them, the information presented to the public does not necessarily represent the opinions expressed by the participants in the poll. There is actually no guarantee to the Canadian people that such polls are taken on a regular sample basis; the people who are asked questions may or may not be representative of Canadians as a whole.
One of the problems facing our people in respect to politics is the fact that an increasing number of people appear to be interested in or concerned with being on the winning side and when a poll is conducted they have a tendency to make the predictions made by a poll come true because they wish to be on
Canada Elections Act
the winning side and so vote in accordance with the indications of these polls. A good example of what can happen from the improper conducting of a poll was the case during an election in the United States. At that time a poll was conducted as to the public opinion with respect to whether the future president of the United States would be a Republican or a Democrat. The general result of the poll suggested the vote would be in favour of the opposition of Mr. Truman to the extent of 12 per cent. On page 663 of volume 2 of "A History of the American People" by Harry J. Carman and Harold C. Syrett, it says:
Throughout the campaign the so-called-and often self-styled-experts, the newspapers, and the professional poll takers were unanimous in their predictions of a sweeping Republican victory.
This volume continues on page 664 as follows:
On the day after the election Truman almost alone could take credit for engineering the most stunning upset in the history of American presidential elections.
This was one case where the poll in fact indicated an incorrect trend although it resulted in little change in the general attitude of the voting public of the United States. It does, however, point out that polls are not necessarily true expressions of opinion and therefore while we should allow them to be taken because they do serve a useful purpose, we should prevent their results from being made public during an election campaign.
We would like to extend this principle to the schools. The practice is becoming quite widely adopted of conducting polls in public schools and in my area the public school children are allowed to conduct an election on election day while they are not allowed to do so three or four days beforehand because this might have some effect on the opinion expressed on election day. In British Columbia some action has been taken on this matter and an amendment has been introduced to the elections act in that province, namely section 168, which reads as follows:
168. No person, corporation, or organization shall, after the issue of the writ for any election, take any straw vote which will, prior to the election, distinguish the political opinions of the voters in any electoral district.
This was passed in 1939 and has worked very satisfactorily in British Columbia and we are suggesting similar legislation be introduced by the government of Canada. I am quite sure there will be some expression of opinion on this matter and I will not now take any more time but will allow the house to decide whether it will vote on this bill today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting for a new member to examine bills introduced by opposition parties during a first session.
While we are considering the bill introduced by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), I should like to say that in the first place, we should ask ourselves whether the action taken by the hon. member opposite has not been influenced by the results of the last federal election. While the result of the last election campaign was not very favourable to the party he represents, I trust the hon. member for Timiskaming is rather more interested in the principle at stake. I must therefore congratulate him on introducing this bill.
We must realize that the straw votes or public opinion polls conducted prior to election campaigns cannot indicate with any degree of accuracy the actual facts and the state of public opinion.
We know, and the hon. member did point that out at the beginning of his remarks, that in certain countries the results of public opinion polls conducted for the purpose of determining public feeling prior to voting day were not vindicated by the results of the vote itself.
We also are aware of the fact that election campaigns should be carried out in an atmosphere of calm and serenity. We see by the Canada Elections Act, particularly with ref-ference to those days which immediately precede voting day, that the lawmaker's intention was that the people be put in a position to analyse with as great a degree as possible of calm and serenity the various political platforms submitted to their approval as well as to judge at their proper value the men who are seeking to obtain endorsation through universal suffrage. That is why I feel convinced that the proposed legislation introduced by the hon. member opposite is very much in line with that atmosphere of calm, serenity and balance in which any election campaign should, in fact, take place.
It can be claimed that straw votes, public opinion polls are more likely to foster the ambitions of the various political parties than to enlighten public opinion to any substantial degree.
I remember, among other things, that in the province of Quebec, during the last election, a certain newspaper asked its readers to send in their opinions with regard to the probable outcome of the vote. This newspaper having compiled various letters and communications from its friends and subscribers proceeded to publish first rate articles -in large type, of course-in an attempt to

show that the views of those friends and subscribers were, in fact, a true indication of public opinion in a certain area, in the province or even in the country.
This shows that straw votes, or public opinion polls are not based on a fair sample of citizens, a representative cross-section of the people, but that on the contrary, especially when they are conducted by newspapers or propaganda agencies and involve friends and subscribers of those organizations, they provide results which have very little to do, if anything, with the current state of public feeling.
Indeed, we have seen that, in the course of history, some countries ruled by dictators, have benefited from such artifice. If we recall Hitler's career, we remember that he prepared his elections by resorting to such manoeuvres and that he did so with a great deal of acumen and flexibility, so that the voter was not left to himself facing his conscience, and weighing with a calm and balanced mind his final opinion of the actual value of party programs or candidates. Well, by such excessive campaigning, he influenced voters and public opinion single-mindedly as to the actual value of his political program.
Here in Canada political parties favouring the universal vote are placed in a position perhaps more peculiar than in other countries, for our economy varies according to the area where we live. Because of Canada's geographical conditions, Canadians face different issues. For instance those living in the west or in British Columbia have to solve problems relating to industry and fishing. In the more central part of the west we have the issues of farming and agriculture. In Ontario and in the province of Quebec there are problems concerning industry and labour, while in the maritimes the problems of thermal stations, of fisheries and of shipbuilding take the spotlight.
We see therefore that because of the geographical configuration of our country, the Canadian citizen who wants to form his own opinion and study the various policies, must first consider every issue from various angles, always taking into account the province or the area where he lives. Now those propaganda organizations talk only in figures, without giving any substantial or constructive idea. They are often content to publish figures in support of this or that party. Needless to say that when a survey is limited to a certain district, the citizens of that area, because of geographical differences will not always be able to share, with regard to our commonweal, the opinion of those other Canadians who live outside that area or at the other end of the country.

That is why we have witnessed during the last election a propoganda which did not adequately inform our people. I believe those publicity and propaganda agencies should rather try to explain the economic and industrial problems of Canada, instead of just luring people with figures which do not give a real picture of the Canadian way of thinking.
In the last election campaign-as would have been the case in any other-Canadian citizens should have been informed of the problems facing the country. This way, Canadians could have been told of the situation of the textile industry, which is vital for many cities in the province of Quebec. In fact, several cities of that province depend upon the textile industry, as it employs more than
47,000	workers. Those propaganda agencies could have provided our citizens of the areas concerned with interesting data, constructive ideas about that industry, explaining the origin, history and cause of the slump, while suggesting at the same thing the appropriate remedies to improve the situation in that field.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that during an election campaign, the propaganda organizations should endeavour to keep Canadians informed of the very basis of our government, its various fields of activity, as well as about the Canadian constitution of 1867.
I feel that several members of the house realized, during the last election campaign -as was the case in previous campaigns- that very few Canadians are aware of the provisions under which the Canadian constitution allows the federal government to exercise powers in certain fields, while granting provinces perfect freedom of action in others, and putting municipalities in a position to meet their respective obligations. Consequently, propaganda agencies should endeavour, during any election campaign, to inform the Canadian citizen, so that he may be aware of the industrial and economic problems facing his country, as well as of the constitution which governs him. He would then be in a better position to assess the political platform of the various parties because, after all, propaganda should seek to educate, and this it cannot do by merely showing figures that do not mean much for, while they might reveal trends or policies, they do not explain the various grievances upon which the Canadian population is called upon to decide.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure -as I said at the beginning of my remarks- in congratulating the hon. member for Timis-kaming, for raising, by means of his bill, a principle which is well in line with the general principles of the elections act, which demand that, during any election campaign, both male and female electors enjoy full
Canada Elections Act
freedom of thought and full liberty of conscience, in order that they may better understand the Canadian problems and the political platforms which are presented to them in those important circumstances.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by taking part in the discussion of this bill I shall most probably ruffle the feelings of my colleague from Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard).
If I correctly understand the purpose of Bill C-19, it merely consists in amending the Canada Elections Act by adding the following sentence:
After the issue of the writ for an election, or after the dissolution of parliament or the occurrence of a vacancy in consequence of which a writ for an election is eventually issued-
That, as I see it, is what the sponsor of this bill wishes to add to section 108, subsection 1, chapter 23 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, which at present reads as follows:
No person, company or corporation shall, in any province and before the hour of closing of the polls in such province, publish the result or purported result of a straw vote or poll of the political opinions of the electors or any of them in any electoral district or districts in Canada, whether such publication is by radio broadcast, or by newspaper, news-sheet, poster, bill-board, handbill or in any other manner; any person contravening the provisions of this subsection (and in the case of a company or corporation, any person responsible for the contravention thereof) is guilty of an illegal practice and of an offence against this act.
Mr. Speaker, if I correctly understand this bill, it seems to me superfluous because it makes no change whatever in the elections act; it merely adds a few words to the provisions of that legislation. I feel that our opponents will certainly not achieve their purpose by amending the act along the lines of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Timiskaming.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, we were happy to read in last week's newspapers that according to a poll conducted recently in this country, the Conservative party is increasingly popular. This has had no effect whatever on the results of the March 31 elections.
I think I have a pretty fair idea of the real purpose behind the proposed amendment. I wonder, not without some anxiety, if our hon. friends of the "group"-to use the words of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch)-are not somewhat afraid of public opinion. Knowing full well that they do not enjoy a great deal of popularity in this country, they obviously must make every

Canada Elections Act
attempt to limit, among the people of this country, the results of the very restricted popularity they enjoy.
I would feel remiss in my duty, Mr. Speaker, if I were not to pay some tribute to the value of public opinion polls. I am convinced that many of my colleagues in this house share my views on this matter. Public opinion polls are the basis of true democracy, devoid of any taint of socialism, whatever form this socialism may take. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I believe that public opinion polls serve to prove the freedom of opinion enjoyed in a truly democratic country and that, further, it confirms the liberty of the press in this country.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are some of the reasons why I do not welcome the proposed amendment to the Canada Elections Act. By proposing such a legislation, it is obvious that certain political persons can gain a certain amount of newspaper publicity.
If our friends believe they are harmed by those public opinion polls, all they have to do is to ask for enforcement of sub-section 1 of section 67 of the Canada Elections Act. They will find there essential factors protecting their popularity, if they feel concerned.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that by bringing this amendment to the Canada Elections Act there is any other purpose than to suggest very sincerely that those reports are liable to influence people. There certainly is no undue influence in those popular polls because section 67 provides for such cases during an election campaign, and could be invoked to forbid their publication. If my hon. friends of the small group of the opposition will allow me, I will read that section:
67. (1) Every person is guilty of the corrupt practice of undue influence and of an indictable offence against this Act punishable as provided in this Act, who, directly or indirectly, by himself or by any other person on his behalf, makes use of, or threatens to make use of, any force, violence or restraint, or inflicts, or threatens the infliction.
I will not read the rest of the section. I only wanted to draw a parallel between the provision of section 108 of the act and the undue influence to which my hon. friends seemed to refer.
Mr. Speaker, I do not see how those public opinion polls can in any way influence the vote. I have more confidence than that in the integrity of the Canadian electorate. I am convinced that nobody would let his vote be influenced by glancing, on occasion, with a
bit of discretion, at the results of those popular polls. People want to be informed, and I believe that it is the duty of the newspapers to inform them. A poll does not constitute propaganda. The report of a public opinion poll is only the announcement that, in some measure, a percentage of the population declared itself for or against a political party or politician.
I do not think that these polls can prejudice our friends in any way because people very often consider not so much the results of such popular polls but rather the programs and the candidates. That is why the Canadian people sent 208 Conservatives to this house in the last election. Therefore we see that the result of the public poll taken before the last election gave the facts and that the survey was neither inaccurate nor dishonest. I heard the hon. member who moved this bill talking of criticisms directed against the Gallup poll after the election campaign of Mr. Truman in 1948. However this just proves that such surveys of public opinion do not in any way change individual conviction, for even if those polls did not favour former president Truman, the result showed that the personal opinion of each voter was worth more than such public survey.
Mr. Speaker, I made these remarks because, though I am not opposed to this bill, I do not see any use in it. Without wanting to influence anybody, I believe this bill should not have been submitted to this house this afternoon.

This resolution provides for the introduction of a bill to make certain amendments to the Financial Administration Act. I notice most of these amendments are somewhat minor in character, generally


speaking, but there is one amendment provided for that does interest this group particularly, and I judge from the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River interests his group also, and that is the amendment to clarify the circumstances in which special warrants signed by the governor general may be issued.
I cannot read the word "clarified" without thinking of the former member for Cape Breton South because that was a favourite phrase of his when he was in this house, when he was trying to get the government to clear up some misunderstanding with respect to legislation. I believe, from the point of view of this group, this is an important part of this legislation, particularly in view of the government's action last session and the large amounts that were passed under governor general's warrants and in view also of the failure of the government to include a certain warrant in the estimates of citizenship and immigration. I am sure the minister will recall the afternoon and evening debate that occurred on the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration because of the failure of the government to include in those estimates a certain estimate provided for by a governor general's warrant. I presume that while at the time the efforts of this group in that respect seemed somewhat futile, and the response from the government side of the house was negative, the introduction of this resolution would indicate that some afterthought caused the government to give a second consideration to their former actions.
As I said before, we are interested in this question of clarifying the circumstances in which a special warrant signed by the governor general may be issued. I think not only we in this group but a good many members of this house and, during the last year, a very great many people in the country, were seriously concerned about this matter. I am not questioning for one moment that the government did find itself in somewhat unusual and particular circumstances, and found it necessary on occasion to issue these governor general's warrants for very large sums of money. But the circumstances were such as to cause a certain amount of eyebrow raising and concern across this country by people who give consideration to the proper recognition of the rights of parliament, and a recognition of the proper procedures, and so on. We are very glad, therefore, the government has introduced this resolution.
However, to indicate the concern, I am simply going to quote from an article that appeared in one newspaper, and similar

articles appeared in newspapers across Canada. I should like to quote from the Ottawa Citizen, February 17,	1958, shortly after
parliament was dissolved and we had all gone home anticipating an election. The article is headed "Bypass Parliament with HalfBillion in Single Warrant". I should like to quote from it briefly:
Largest single governor general's warrant ever issued in Canada-$544,290,332.32-has been received by the Diefenbaker government.
By issuance of a warrant covering practically the full balance of the appropriations asked of parliament in the 1957-58 estimates, and the supplementary estimates to go with them, parliament is being bypassed completely.
The only way parliament will have to deal with this half-billion is when public acounts are presented more than a year hence, after all the money is spent, unless the government elected March 31 chooses to get parliamentary approval in some other way-
No additions to the estimates have been included in it but there are certain important deletions from them including one of $103 million which former finance minister Harris put in to cover the deficit on the old age security fund. This $103 million will not now show in the accounts for the current fiscal year and will either increase the surplus or reduce the deficit for the final accounting on the fiscal year.
The government is said to have decided that there was no precedent for covering such an expenditure by issuance of a governor general's warrant.
Then, there is one more short paragraph headed "Difference in 1940 Warrant":
One has to go back to 1940, the first full year of the war, to get a warrant of a size even remotely approaching the present one. But even there there was this important difference:
The 1940 warrant did not cover expenditures up to the end of the fiscal year which meant that when parliament was asked to vote the money for the last month it could examine every item in detail if it wished.
I quote that to indicate the criticisms that occurred in newspapers across this country and which I think did reflect the concern of thinking people with these procedures, and with the securing of governor general's warrants shortly after parliament had been dissolved for such large sums of money.
I said, Mr. Chairman, we were going to be very brief at this stage. We look forward to the bill, and we will reserve the greater part of our discussion until we have the bill in our hands, and after we have had an opportunity for close scrutiny of the proposals contained in this measure.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE DELETION OF CERTAIN ACCOUNTS, CLARIFY ISSUE OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S WARRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Before this resolution carries may I say that in so far as it deals with methods of tidying up some of the financial procedures that have been carried on in the past I think it is a useful bill and will be supported on this side. But as has already been indicated, we have a special interest in that part of the resolution which deals
Financial Administration Act with a very important, and certainly last January, a very controversial question, that is governor general's warrants.
We should like to be assured, and we hope the bill will give us that assurance, that procedures will be laid down which will ensure that these warrants can be given full parliamentary consideration in the future, and given the consideration which we felt was not given last January. I should add that this kind of consideration was always given when we were in office because I think we were scrupulous in insisting that when governor general's warrants were utilized there was a method adopted by which parliament could always consider and pass upon them. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River before six o'clock did suggest that perhaps it would be a good thing to have this bill go before the public accounts committee for scrutiny. No doubt the minister will be considering that suggestion.
But apart from that, Mr. Chairman, we remind the minister, as no doubt he was reminded before six o'clock, that there is a specific statement on the record by the Prime Minister to the effect that the committee on public accounts would be set up for the purpose, amongst other things, of considering governor general's warrants. I refer to page 34 of Hansard for May 13, 1958 where the Prime Minister said:
We intend to set up this committee;-
That is the public accounts committee.
-we intend to have an examination of the expenditures made under governor general's warrants.
He must have meant an examination before that committee. He went on to say this:
It is not a question of amount. There were governor general's warrants issued and passed and my reading of the record does not indicate that the stand we are going to take whereby the expenditures were made available to a committee of the house for complete examination was taken in the past.
Hence from that statement of the Prime Minister we have the right to assume that if and when this bill is passed the governor general's warrants with which we are concerned at the present time and which have not been considered by this house will be referred, as the first item or as an early item of business, to the public accounts committee as stated by the Prime Minister on May 13 last. We should like to get from the minister an assurance that this course will be followed.

Financial Administration Act on that occasion. He is reading that statement as saying that the warrants are going to be referred to the public accounts committee. If you will have regard to what was said on May 13 and May 14 by myself on the same subject, Mr. Chairman, you will see set out in some detail the procedure that is intended to be followed.
Any expenditure that is made, whether in pursuance of an appropriation by act of parliament or in pursuance of an appropriation by warrant, of course, falls within the ambit of review by the public accounts committee when reported to the house in the public accounts in the ordinary course. Certainly the expenditures made by warrant in the months of February and March as well as in April and the first half of May of this year will in due course fall within the ambit of the public accounts committee after the Auditor General has completed his normal audit. That is a different matter, however, from the task that will confront the house at the present session of dealing with warrants in a different context.
As was indicated by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River this afternoon, what is looked for and what I indicated in my remarks on May 13 and 14 as the intention of the government is to bring in a measure which will deal with the supply for the year 1957-58 including the warrants in a manner that will afford the house the fullest opportunity to go over the supply item by item. That is another measure. It is not the measure before us now.
What we are dealing with now is a resolution contemplating the amendment of the Financial Administration Act, for the future, dealing with the kind of situation we have encountered this year and to clarify the law in all respects so that in future neither parliament nor government will be left in any question as to what is the course that should be followed in a situation where it is necessary to provide for a needed expenditure under urgent circumstances by governor general's warrants. The situation about which the Leader of the Opposition was talking is one that is quite outside the scope of the present resolution. I expect within a few days to be bringing before the house a resolution which will deal with that subject and which will afford to hon. members an opportunity of reviewing the items that enter into the supply for 1957-58, including warrants.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE DELETION OF CERTAIN ACCOUNTS, CLARIFY ISSUE OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S WARRANTS, ETC.

-we intend to have an examination of the expenditures made under governor general's warrants.
The only expenditures made under governor general's warrants about which he could have been thinking were those made by the government in the last twelve months. Those must have been the expenditures which he said would be referred to this committee which was about to be set up. My hon. friend said that he is going to introduce another resolution on this subject which will indicate how these governor general's warrants are to be dealt with in order to ensure that parliament will be given the full right of discussion. All I am suggesting-and perhaps he will bear this in mind-is that in that resolution we would expect some provision to be made for the discussion of these warrants in the public accounts committee because that is what we were led to believe would happen when the Prime Minister made that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE DELETION OF CERTAIN ACCOUNTS, CLARIFY ISSUE OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S WARRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: I think I should remind my hon. friend that accounts are referred to the public accounts committee under the procedures of this house only after they have been audited by the Auditor General. Materials (not including grease or lubricating oils) consumed or expended directly in the process of manufacture or production of goods.

[The Chairman.]
that fuel so consumed is consumed in production if the engine it drives is used in production but it was always construed that the fuel should be subject to sales tax and indeed until last October this clause was always interpreted as meaning that such fuel was made taxable by that part of the schedule that deals with lighting and heating because that section specifically excluded fuel for use in internal combustion engines. A situation arose last October which brought this matter into very direct focus. It concerned fuel oil used in internal combustion engines. In other words, we have introduced the amendment which the committee has already approved in clause l(b)(v), where the diesel fuel oil is being used in generating electricity and has been sold to or imported by municipalities for their own use and not for resale.

Item 12 deals, as the committee knows, with a very important matter indeed. It is concerned with a problem that really transcends the particular item itself. I refer to the problem of maintaining in this country a Canadian periodical literature. I am not at all sure-and perhaps the minister will give us his views on this matter-that the particular method used by the previous government to deal with this problem was the right approach to it. I am not sure whether or not it would have solved the problem if it had been continued. But there is no doubt in the world that the problem remains. The repeal of this particular tax does not do anything to solve the problem one way or another.
This problem, I suggest, is unparalleled in any other country of which I am aware. I do not know of any situation similar to that which exists between our country and our neighbour, the United States, in so far as the influence of periodical literature of one country upon another is concerned. That problem of course arises from the fact that we 17 million Canadians live alongside a country of 175 million people who speak the same language as do most of us and with whom we have a very close, friendly and intimate relationship with them which we desire to maintain. Our manner of living is the same. All this encourages the entry of periodical literature into Canada from across the border. It has also encouraged in recent years the production in this country of what are called the Canadian editions of United States periodicals. The problem, of course, would not exist if United States periodical literature and other forms of literature from 57071-3-180
Excise Tax Act
that nation were printed in a language different from our own but that is not the case. The result is obvious if one looks at a bookstand in any Canadian town or city, but the common language manifests itself in this particular way I have just mentioned, the Canadian editions of United States periodicals.
This tax was meant to deal with that particular problem. I suggest that the increase of periodical literature from the United States into this country and the growing influence of that literature upon our people does have a relationship to our desires to develop a distinct and self-reliant Canadian identity- what we call Canadianism. The report of the Massey commission in 1951 had something to say on this subject, and this is a problem which I suggest is not being faced by the repeal of this tax. The Massey report had this to say:
Every intelligent Canadian acknowledges his debt to the United States for excellent films, radio programs and periodicals. But the price may be excessive-
The Canadian periodical cannot in its turn invade the American market; for Americans, it seems, simply do not know enough about Canada to appreciate Canadian material. Our periodicals cannot hold their own except in their limited and unprotected market, nine million English-speaking readers_
That was in 1951 but there would be more today.
It cannot be denied . . . that a vast and disproportionate amount of material coming from a single alien source may stifle rather than stimulate our own creative effort-
Officially we have no concern with newspapers or magazines . . . Nonetheless, it would seem to us incongruous ... to leave unmentioned the newspaper and periodical press of Canada which provides most of the reading matter of most Canadians and which is still probably the chief source of knowledge to Canadians of their country and of one another.
Now that is the situation which confronted the Massey commission in 1951 and the situation exists today in a new form through the development of this device-if I may call it that-of Canadian editions of United States periodicals. It was to deal with this problem that the tax was imposed two years ago and I suggest that while this may not have been the most effective way of dealing with the matter-and the minister might give us his opinion on that-the problem nevertheless remains and something should be done about it because it is not an ordinary form of competition. This tax was not meant to interfere and did not interfere in any way, shape or form with competition, in the ordinary sense of the word, between Canadian periodicals and United States periodicals. It was, as I say, to deal with the problem of Canadian editions of periodicals coming from across the border and that is a problem with which it was particularly difficult to deal. I presented

Excise Tax Act
special difficulties for Canadian publishers and it has been alleged-and a good deal of evidence has been brought forward to support this allegation-that these so-called Canadian editions could never have developed and flourished in Canada on the advertising rates which were in fact charged if it had not been for the parent magazines upon which they could lean. It appeared that part of the expenses of the Canadian edition had been met by the larger publication in the United States and in that particular sense-although I certainly would not want to push this parallel too far-it might be alleged that this was a form of journalistic dumping as it was an unfair advantage given to the Canadian editions and the United States magazines. However, as I say, I do not wish to push this parallel too far, but whatever the reason may have been these Canadian editions have occupied an increasing proportion of the reading time of the Canadian public over recent years. This has constituted a special threat to Canadian periodical literature.
So far as this tax is concerned, as I have said, it did not make the position of the Canadian magazine publishers any less competitive than in the past and it was not meant to have and has not had the slightest effect on the United States magazines coming into Canada. In fact the two Canadian editions which have most benefited from this situation -Time and Reader's Digest-have not lost any substantial volume of advertising but perhaps it is correct to say that it has prevented an increase in the volume of advertising and in the circulation of these magazines in Canada. Perhaps it is also correct to say that it has prevented the appearance in this country of new so-called Canadian editions of United States periodicals. If this were a question of straightforward competition between one Canadian magazine and another I do not think anybody would have any interest in defending the position of any one magazine against another, but this is a question of competition in Canada from so-called Canadian editions of United States publications, some of the expenses of which are met in the United States. That is a very special problem.
I am informed, furthermore, that since the announcement of the repeal of this tax in the budget speech two United States magazines have announced their intentions of, in one case publishing a Canadian edition and, in the other case, resuming the publication of a Canadian edition which had been suspended when the tax was put into effect a couple of years ago and that yet another United States magazine, which I believe was on the point of publishing a Canadian edition at that time, is

now reconsidering the possibilities in that regard.
Mr. Chairman, I merely call the attention of the minister and the government to this particular problem. Surely it is nothing that we can contemplate with any degree of equanimity, the disappearance or serious diminution of Canadian bona fide periodical literature. Surely the vision of Canada cannot include a periodical literature circulating in this country which is alien in spirit, in thought, in origin and indeed, perhaps, in some other respects. Therefore I ask the minister whether in repealing this tax as they are proposing to do in this particular resolution, the government is aware of this problem which I have attempted to outline and if he is aware of the problem, what steps does the government propose to take to meet it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. gentleman that the government was aware of this problem long before this evening. I yield to no one in my concern for the flourishing growth in Canada of a Canadian culture. The problem is a very difficult one in a country like ours with 17 million people alongside a country of 175 million and where the cultural influence of the United States is exerted with very great strength, persistency and constancy on the Canadian public in very many forms. I yield to no man in my desire to see a Canadian culture express itself in every reasonable form, and that will certainly include Canadian culture as reflected in Canadian magazines.
However, it is a far cry from a position of that kind, which I trust and believe is shared by all hon. members of the house, to defending this tax. This tax was brought forward two years ago in the guise of a measure that would assist in the preservation of the Canadian magazine industry. It never was a sound method of assisting the Canadian magazine industry. As a tax it was open to all of the criticisms that were levelled against it in all parts of Canada. It was an attempt to use the taxing power for a purpose for which, in my respectful submission, the taxing power ought not to have been used.
The problem was there before 1956. The government of that day had done nothing else about the problem. In 1956 it brought in the magazine tax. That tax was not a sound way of dealing with the problem, and we resisted it at the time. Nevertheless, the government of that day chose to impose this tax. What has happened in the two years during which this tax has been in effect has confirmed everything that we said about it at the time. What we indicated then might be expected to flow from the tax

has, indeed, been realized. We were given to understand that there were two United States magazines in particular, that had Canadian editions which were going to feel the weight of this tax. We said then that those magazines would not feel the weight of this tax but that it would be Canadian magazines that would feel its results. That has been proved to be the fact, because the revenues of those companies from their advertising sources in Canada have not been diminished, but evidently the total budgets of Canadian firms that are advertising, so far as their advertising expenditures have gone into magazines or other media which are strictly Canadian in their origin, have been abated accordingly.
And so this tax measure was not of benefit to those whom it was claimed it was going to help. In repealing this measure, as we invite the house to do, we are asking the house to deal with the tax measure on its merits. The tax measure was not sound in the first place, and it does not deserve to be continued.
The Leader of the Opposition asked what the government is going to do about the problem. I may say that the problem has not changed in its essential aspects from what it was when the hon. gentleman who now leads the opposition was in office, and from what it was before 1956 when this tax was imposed. We have received representations from the periodic press association and others in connection with this tax, and in every case we have tried to show an understanding of the problem and a sympathy with the difficulties that have confronted the Canadian magazine industry, and we have sought some other ways of meeting the problem. We have invited them to put forward suggestions for meeting the problem, but nothing has yet been forthcoming that will meet the problem without either creating other and exaggerated forms of the same problem, or discriminations that cannot be tolerated, or measures that are of the nature of the present tax and which therefore cannot be supported.
I would be happy to receive from the Leader of the Opposition, or from any hon. member regardless of party, any suggestions at all for measures that can be of assistance in relation to the larger problem of the position of media of Canadian culture in Canada. I draw a line here, Mr. Chairman. We are not prepared, as we made quite clear two years ago in the debate on this measure when the former government proposed to impose the tax, to entertain suggestions that contemplate any interference with the flow of ideas, and a great many of the suggestions that have been made, all of which we have 57071-3-180J
Excise Tax Act
carefully considered, have been suggestions that would interfere in some form or other, perhaps not altogether blatantly, with the free flow of ideas. Undeniably there is a problem, and we will be glad to have suggestions as to anything that is sound and acceptable in giving assistance to meet the problem. But so far as this tax is concerned, it never was any contribution in any degree whatever to assisting in this problem, and therefore on its merits this tax, in my respectful submission, should be abolished.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I am grateful to the minister for suggesting that members of the house should provide him with some ideas which may help him in the solution of this problem, the importance of which he said he recognizes, and I can assure him that any ideas which may come from this side of the house will not be such as to interfere with what he called the free flow of ideas across the border, because that is certainly not in our minds. If that were the solution to the problem, all we would have to do would be to put obstacles in the way of the admission of the United States magazines into Canada, and we do not want to do that. But the minister in his speech apparently did not make any distinction between news magazines as such coming across the border and United States magazines, news magazines like Time, putting a couple of Canadian pages on the front and a maple leaf on the cover and being sold in Canada as Canadian editions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: My hon. friend is aware about the printing in Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Yes, I am aware of that but I am also aware of the fact-and the minister must surely recognize it-that the editorial comment and news and opinion-because it is a magazine of opinion-is United States opinion on all matters with which the magazine deals except in respect of two or three pages in the front of the magazine. Apart from that it is a United States magazine. I am not complaining about it being a United States magazine and in fact I read many such magazines but it does constitute a separate problem by calling itself a Canadian edition of a United States magazine.
Therefore, the problem we are faced with, as I see it, is not the admission into this country of United States magazines concerning which the minister asked us to address ourselves and provide any ideas we may have in connection with the matter. On the contrary the problem is specifically one of Canadian editions of United States magazines. He has not given us the benefit of his views as to that problem or as to whether it is

Excise Tax Act
serious and what perhaps might be done about it. He did say, however, that the problem existed before 1956 when this particular action was taken and that nothing was done about it until 1956. That is true, but the problem had not existed many years before 1956. The development of Canadian editions of United States magazines is a comparatively new growth in our periodical literature. I do not know exactly how far back it goes but I feel sure it does not go back much beyond 1956.
The minister in his statement said that this tax was not effective, that it was of no value or use. I am not defending the tax or attacking it. I am merely trying to elucidate the problem and get from the minister some appreciation of it and perhaps an indication that something will be done about it.
The minister said the situation is the same now as it was when the tax was imposed and that the tax had done nothing to help solve the problem. That, of course, is not the opinion of the periodical publishers in Canada of whom I have knowledge. They are of the opinion that this tax had been of some help to them. The figures reveal that in 1956 these two publications with Canadian editions, Time and Reader's Digest, had 49.9 per cent of the total number of advertising pages carried in all magazines published in Canada and a year later, in 1957, that had dropped to 49.5 per cent rather than increased. So perhaps the tax may have had that particular effect in stopping the increase in those two magazines so far as advertising pages are concerned. The same would not be true in terms of advertising revenue because the advertising rates were increased.
It also had another effect which I mentioned in my other statement. We are told that the imposition of this tax did prevent the appearance in Canada of additional Canadian editions of United States magazines since, in the last two years, none of these has appeared. We are informed now that two of them are forthcoming. One is to reappear and a third publication is contemplating a Canadian edition. While this tax may not have been the right way to deal with the problem perhaps it did have the particular result of precluding additional Canadian editions and if it is to be dropped I would hope something could be found to replace it which would make a contribution to the solution of this problem which is a very real problem affecting the Canadian nation.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Just for the record, Mr. Chairman, I should like to inquire if the situation has changed. My last information was to the effect that Reader's Digest is

printed in Canada but I understand that Time is printed outside of Canada.

Reader's Digest is printed in Canada and has been throughout the period of which we are speaking. As far as Time is concerned, I am not sure.
