subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I believe that the opinions of the minister and his concern for Canadian culture are more than merely pious expressions but I do feel that the Leader of the Opposition left with him a conundrum on which I hope he will exercise the government's initiative rather than taking a passive course. The remarks made by the minister sounded to me somewhat like the tradition established by William Lyon Mackenzie King of saying, "You bring your ideas to me". If this is a difficult problem, what do we have a government for if it cannot come forward with a proposal that will help the Canadian periodical press? It is too easy to say to hon. members of the opposition that they should come forward with their ideas. The people of Canada put these hon. gentlemen where they are because they were supposed to have ideas.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I do not share that criticism. I think it is a highly encouraging thing that the government realizes there are ideas on this side of the house and would like to take advantage of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I said the same thing to various groups whether on one side or the other who came to see me about this. We want their suggestions and the more helpful they are the more we are grateful.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
In this case, Mr. Chairman, there is a difference in the form of the resolutions. In respect of the amendments to each of the other three acts there was one resolution with various paragraphs in them. In the case of the proposed amendments to the Customs Tariff, however, there is a series of individual resolutions. They were put in that form before the house because most of them arise out of individual reports of the tariff board. They are rather different in nature and it was felt this would be of assistance to the committee of the whole in dealing with them.
For instance, the first resolution is one simply dealing with amendments of definitions. The second resolution deals with certain amendments affecting zinc and zinc products which arise out of a particular report of the tariff board. The third resolution pertains to iron and steel products and the amendments arise out of another report of the tariff board. Resolution No. 4 also arises out of the tariff board report on iron and steel. No. 5 arises out of the report of the tariff board on pipes and tubes and so on. We are, therefore, dealing with a series of different subjects which are the occasion of proposed amendments to the Customs Tariff.
The Depuiy Chairman: Well, the first resolution is at the top of page 6 and continues down to (m). Shall the resolution carry?

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the minister in presenting these items in sections according to the tariff board recommendations and leaving to the last the miscellaneous items that we usually encounter is using a good system. At page 1247 of Hansard the minister made some reference to these resolutions that would come before us when he was delivering his budget speech. The first package group, if I may call it such, would be the zinc and zinc products group, and I find he had something to say about it rather different from what is referred to in any of the other groups. He was more positive. He said:
These proposed tariff changes constitute a balanced package. On balance the proposed changes do not involve any increase in the Canadian tariff on zinc and zinc products.
With respect to the other packages, I take it that on balance he could not go that far. I am speaking in a general way-I do not want to delay the committee-but I want to show the contrast. He said, with respect to pipes and tubes:
A major result of these changes will be to make more effective the protection which it affords to Canadian producers.

Customs Tariff
Then, with respect to the basic iron and steel products, he concluded his reference to that by saying:
I understand that Canadian steel producers consider the new schedule to be a decided improvement over the old one.
There is nothing that I think is more important to most members of the committee these days, Mr. Chairman, than the matter of trade. I think the expression of Sir Wilfrid Laurier is just as valid now as it was when he said it. He said:
Canada has need of three things. The first is markets; the second is markets and the third is markets.
I think most of us realize today that a number of our products are subject to the general agreement on tariffs and trade and we all very well realize that trade is a two-way street. I quoted the Prime Minister in my budget speech and he explained very carefully at Brantford that if we are cutting off trade in the nature of imports we are bound to find that some of our opportunities for exports will suffer, and that is what I think will concern the committee as we go through these items.
It is very difficult for the committee to determine, unless the minister will draw it to our attention, which items of the many that we have-several hundred of them-in front of us were bound items and have something to do with the trading that necessarily takes place when it is the intention of the government to increase the tariff on something that is bound under the GATT agreement.
The minister said on June 17 that there were other negotiations pending respecting GATT. We, I am sure, will be interested to know to what extent they relate to some of the items that we have in front of us, if they relate at all. I am thinking particularly of the negotiations that have been initiated with respect to fresh fruit and vegetables. The minister said: "Negotiations have been initiated." Again he said: "I hope that these will soon lead to an agreement on a more satisfactory schedule of duties." Well, as someone said, of course, the question is always, more satisfactory to whom? In all of these resolutions that we have in front of us I think that is the basis of the inquiry of the committee. What is the balance or is it more satisfactory to one segment of our economy than another.
I wonder whether the minister would care to tell us about the progress of negotiations with respect to fresh fruit and vegetables, particularly as it relates to the possibility of anything coming before the present session?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF

Let me say at once there is nothing in these resolutions that

touches on fresh fruit and vegetables and I do not think it is proper to lead off into a matter of that kind. It was mentioned in the budget speech; it was discussed in the budget debate. If my hon. friend wishes to ask me questions of that kind on my estimates I shall be glad to deal with them. I do not think it is proper in this series of resolutions to deal with something that is not touched on in them at all. I should be glad to deal with it on my estimates.

speechtext: I would like to hear from the minister as to the progress. Certainly, it is appropriate on the bill, but without delaying the committee I think the minister might just save time by telling us. He lost time last week, I think, by being a bit truculent.
